entities.name: Henri II de Rohan
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Henri II de Rohan (1579–1638), Duke of Rohan and Prince of Léon, emerged as the preeminent military and political leader of the Huguenots, French Calvinist Protestants, during the tumultuous early 17th century. His life, spanning the reigns of Henri IV and Louis XIII, was inextricably linked to the religious wars that continued to plague France despite the Edict of Nantes. Rohan’s strategic acumen and unwavering commitment to the Protestant cause, particularly during the final Huguenot rebellions from 1621 to 1629, made him a pivotal figure in the consolidation of royal power under Cardinal Richelieu and the eventual suppression of independent Protestant strongholds within France. His actions resonated across Europe, influencing the broader religious and geopolitical landscape of the nascent Thirty Years' War.

Born into one of Brittany's most powerful noble families, Rohan inherited leadership of the Huguenot party from his father-in-law, Sully, and his brother, Benjamin de Rohan, Seigneur de Soubise. Following the assassination of Henri IV in 1610, the fragile peace of the Edict of Nantes began to unravel, prompting Rohan to lead the Huguenots in a series of armed uprisings against the crown. He orchestrated formidable defenses of cities like Montauban (1621) and La Rochelle (1627–1628), demonstrating considerable military skill against royal forces led by Louis XIII and Richelieu. Despite initial successes, the siege and fall of La Rochelle in 1628, followed by the Peace of Alès in 1629, marked the definitive end of Huguenot political and military autonomy in France.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Henri II de Rohan was the last great military leader of the Huguenots, whose prolonged resistance delayed but ultimately failed to prevent the consolidation of royal absolutism in France. His actions and writings provide critical insight into the religious and political struggles of early 17th-century France.
